WITH runs AS (
  SELECT query_id, query_hash, warehouse_size, start_time,
         total_elapsed_ms - queued_ms AS exec_ms
  FROM query_history
  WHERE execution_status = 'SUCCESS'
), baseline AS (
  SELECT query_hash, warehouse_size,
         PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY exec_ms) AS p90,
         COUNT(*) AS runs
  FROM runs
  WHERE start_time >= DATE '{{report_date}}' - {{baseline_days}}
    AND start_time <  DATE '{{report_date}}'
  GROUP BY query_hash, warehouse_size
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_runs}}
)
SELECT r.query_id, r.query_hash, r.warehouse_size, r.exec_ms,
       ROUND(b.p90::numeric, 1) AS baseline_p90_ms,
       b.runs AS baseline_runs
FROM runs r
JOIN baseline b ON b.query_hash = r.query_hash AND b.warehouse_size = r.warehouse_size
WHERE r.start_time >= DATE '{{report_date}}'
  AND r.start_time <  DATE '{{report_date}}' + 1
  AND r.exec_ms > {{factor}} * b.p90
  AND r.exec_ms - b.p90 >= {{min_excess_ms}}
ORDER BY r.query_hash, r.exec_ms DESC, r.query_id;

Explanation. One CTE defines a run once (successful, execution time without the queue), so the baseline and the report day cannot disagree about it. The baseline is a plain aggregate over a half-open window that ends where the report day starts, so a regression on the report day cannot raise its own threshold. HAVING drops fingerprints with too little history; the inner join then drops their report-day runs. The comparison uses the unrounded p90; only the output is rounded. Below Very Hard each fingerprint runs on one warehouse size, so grouping by (query_hash, warehouse_size) is the same as grouping by query_hash; at Very Hard the size is part of the baseline's key and the absolute-excess guard applies. A candidate who groups by query_hash only below Very Hard is correct.

Complexity. One scan, a sort per fingerprint for the percentile (the baseline window is small per fingerprint) and a hash join: O(n log n) in the window's rows. In production the baseline is a daily table (fingerprint, size, day) of pre-aggregated sketches, not a re-scan of N days.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY exec_ms) exists and also works as a window function; APPROX_PERCENTILE uses a sketch and is not exact; DATEADD(day, -7, '2026-09-24'::date); the account-usage query history reports times in milliseconds with queue components in separate columns (check current docs for the exact column set). BigQuery: PERCENTILE_CONT(x, 0.9) OVER (PARTITION BY …) is analytic only, so compute it in a subquery with ANY_VALUE, or use APPROX_QUANTILES(x, 10)[OFFSET(9)] (approximate). Spark SQL: percentile(x, 0.9) is exact with interpolation, percentile_approx is not. MySQL 8: no percentile function; emulate with ROW_NUMBER() and COUNT(*) per fingerprint and interpolate by hand.

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: a run that is slow only because it queued; a fingerprint with exactly min_runs baseline runs and a clear outlier. Hard: failed runs on the report day and failed baseline runs that would lift the p90; a fingerprint with 11 baseline runs, so the p90 is exactly the 10th value, with one run at exactly factor × p90 and one a millisecond above; a run exactly at the window start (needed to reach min_runs) and one a second before it; an outlier in the last second of the report day and a huge run at the next midnight; a fingerprint one run short of the minimum, with another run just before the window. Very Hard: one fingerprint on a large and an extra-small warehouse with a six-fold difference; a tiny fingerprint with a large ratio but a small absolute excess; runs at exactly the minimum excess and one millisecond below it.

Common mistakes. Comparing total_elapsed_ms; including the report day (or all history) in the baseline; a closed window (BETWEEN) or start_time::date comparisons that are right by accident; >= against factor × p90; comparing with the rounded p90; PERCENTILE_DISC, AVG or MEDIAN instead of PERCENTILE_CONT(0.9); counting failed runs; min_runs off by one; mixing warehouse sizes (Very Hard); a window function PERCENTILE_CONT … OVER (PARTITION BY query_hash) over the whole table, which includes the report day.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A slow drift moves the baseline with it; compare the recent p90 with an older reference window (week over week, or a fixed release baseline) and alert on the ratio, or use a change-point test on daily p50/p90. (2) Execution time scales with data scanned; normalise by bytes scanned or partitions scanned, or compare within buckets of scanned size, and say that a "slow" query may simply have been asked a bigger question. (3) Keep a daily per-(fingerprint, size) summary — a t-digest/KLL sketch or a sorted sample — and merge N days of sketches; approximate percentiles are fine for alerting if the error is stated. (4) Page only on a repeated, material regression: several outliers within an hour, an absolute excess, and no warehouse resize or plan change that explains it; measure precision on past alerts before paging anyone.

Rubric anchors. 2: a plausible percentile baseline, but the report day leaks into it, or queue time is included, or the window edges are wrong. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains drift, normalisation by data scanned and an incremental, sketch-based baseline.

Strong signals. Asks what "slow" means before writing SQL; separates queueing (capacity) from execution (the query); keeps the baseline strictly before the report day. Red flags. One global threshold for every query; averaging percentiles of percentiles; treating approximate percentiles as exact.

WITH counted AS (                      -- one row per covered query, paid if any paid entitlement covers it
  SELECT q.query_id, q.listing_id, q.consumer_account, q.query_ts,
         BOOL_OR(e.kind = 'paid') AS is_paid
  FROM listing_queries q
  JOIN listings l ON l.listing_id = q.listing_id
  JOIN entitlements e
    ON e.listing_id = q.listing_id
   AND e.consumer_account = q.consumer_account
   AND e.starts_at <= q.query_ts
   AND (e.ends_at IS NULL OR q.query_ts < e.ends_at)
  WHERE q.consumer_account <> l.provider_account
  GROUP BY q.query_id, q.listing_id, q.consumer_account, q.query_ts
), first_use AS (
  SELECT listing_id, consumer_account,
         date_trunc('month', MIN(query_ts))::date AS first_month
  FROM counted
  GROUP BY listing_id, consumer_account
), monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', query_ts)::date AS month,
         listing_id, consumer_account, BOOL_OR(is_paid) AS paid
  FROM counted
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)
SELECT m.month, m.listing_id,
       COUNT(*)                                       AS consumers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE m.paid)                 AS paid_consumers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT m.paid)             AS trial_only_consumers,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE f.first_month = m.month) AS new_consumers
FROM monthly m
JOIN first_use f USING (listing_id, consumer_account)
WHERE m.month BETWEEN DATE '{{from_month}}' AND DATE '{{to_month}}'
GROUP BY m.month, m.listing_id
ORDER BY m.month, m.listing_id;

Explanation. The interval join keeps only queries an entitlement covers, half-open at ends_at. A query covered by an overlapping trial and paid entitlement appears twice after the join, so the first CTE groups back to one row per query and lets paid win with BOOL_OR. Every metric is then a count at the (month, listing, account) grain, which makes "distinct" structural rather than a COUNT(DISTINCT …) per column, and makes trial-only exactly "not paid". The first counted query per (listing, account) is computed over all history, before the report-month filter, so an account first seen before the window is never new inside it. The provider's own account is excluded before anything else.

Complexity. The interval join is the cost: with an index or clustering on (listing_id, consumer_account) it is a merge of each pair's few entitlements with its queries, O(n log n) overall. Two small aggregations follow.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: BOOLOR_AGG, DATE_TRUNC('month', ts) returns the same type as its input; COUNT_IF. BigQuery: LOGICAL_OR, DATE_TRUNC(DATE(ts), MONTH), COUNTIF; range joins are fine at this size but large interval joins benefit from pre-bucketing. Spark SQL: bool_or, trunc(ts, 'MM'); a range join may need a bin column for performance. MySQL 8: MAX(kind = 'paid'), DATE_FORMAT(ts, '%Y-%m-01'), SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: an account that converts from trial to paid inside one month (paid, not trial-only). Hard: a query exactly at a trial's starts_at (counted) and one exactly at its ends_at in the next month (not counted); queries after a trial lapsed and before any entitlement; a trial and a paid entitlement overlapping with the account's only query of the month in the overlap; the last second of July and the first second of August. Very Hard: the provider's own account with an entitlement and queries in every month; an account first seen in May with queries in June and July (not new in June); an account whose first query is the first second of June (new in June).

Common mistakes. trial_only as "had a trial query" so the columns overlap; BETWEEN starts_at AND ends_at; ignoring NULL ends_at (so open-ended subscriptions vanish); counting the joined rows (an overlap counts the query twice, harmless only with DISTINCT); counting queries with no entitlement; computing "new" after filtering months; letting the provider count as a consumer; COUNT(DISTINCT consumer_account) FILTER (WHERE is_paid) combined with a trial count that is not exclusive.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Cohort by the trial's starts_at month; conversion = accounts with a paid query within 30 days of trial start ÷ cohort size; state that late conversions after 30 days are not counted and that the most recent cohort is incomplete. (2) Precompute daily (listing, account, day, paid) usage: the interval join then runs on a few rows per account per day; cluster by listing and date; months are rollups of days with distinct accounts recomputed (not summed). (3) Counting organisations needs a mapping the provider knows (billing entity) or one the platform exposes; without it, report accounts and say so. (4) Show counts, not query text or columns used; suppress or bucket counts below a threshold (for example fewer than 3 consumers), and never let a filter isolate one consumer.

Rubric anchors. 2: right grain but trial-only overlaps paid, or uncovered queries count, or open-ended entitlements are lost. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also designs the cohort conversion metric and the precomputation, and raises small-count privacy unprompted.

Strong signals. Declares the grain (month, listing, account) before writing; asks how overlapping entitlements resolve; checks that paid plus trial-only equals consumers. Red flags. Summing monthly distinct counts into a quarter; treating the consumption log as if it revealed consumers' queries to the provider.

Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{start_date}} and {{end_date}} are the instance's first and last report days)

WITH spine AS (
  SELECT d::date AS day, d + INTERVAL '1 day' AS snap
  FROM generate_series(DATE '{{start_date}}'::timestamptz,
                       DATE '{{end_date}}'::timestamptz,
                       INTERVAL '1 day') AS d
), ev AS (
  SELECT e.table_name, e.event_ts, e.event_type, e.bytes,
         SUM(CASE e.event_type WHEN 'ADD' THEN e.bytes WHEN 'REMOVE' THEN -e.bytes ELSE 0 END)
           OVER (PARTITION BY e.table_name ORDER BY e.event_ts, e.event_id) AS active_running
  FROM storage_events e
), flows AS (                          -- signed change to active storage; removals as chunks
  SELECT ev.table_name, ev.event_ts,
         CASE WHEN ev.event_type = 'ADD' THEN ev.bytes ELSE 0 END AS added,
         CASE ev.event_type WHEN 'REMOVE' THEN ev.bytes
                            WHEN 'DROP'   THEN ev.active_running   -- everything active at the drop
                            ELSE 0 END AS removed,
         ev.event_ts + make_interval(days => s.retention_days) AS tt_end,
         ev.event_ts + make_interval(days => s.retention_days
                       + CASE WHEN s.table_kind = 'PERMANENT' THEN 7 ELSE 0 END) AS fs_end
  FROM ev
  JOIN table_settings s ON s.table_name = ev.table_name
)
SELECT sp.day, s.table_name,
       COALESCE(SUM(f.added - f.removed), 0)                                       AS active_bytes,
       COALESCE(SUM(f.removed) FILTER (WHERE sp.snap < f.tt_end), 0)               AS time_travel_bytes,
       COALESCE(SUM(f.removed) FILTER (WHERE sp.snap >= f.tt_end AND sp.snap < f.fs_end), 0) AS failsafe_bytes
FROM spine sp
CROSS JOIN table_settings s
LEFT JOIN flows f ON f.table_name = s.table_name AND f.event_ts < sp.snap
GROUP BY sp.day, s.table_name
ORDER BY sp.day, s.table_name;

Explanation. The spine gives every (day, table) pair, including days before a table's first event. Each event becomes a flow: bytes added to active storage, or a removed chunk with the two instants at which it leaves time travel and fail-safe. A chunk removed at t is in time travel while snapshot < t + retention and in fail-safe while t + retention ≤ snapshot < t + retention + F, with F = 0 for transient tables; a chunk past fs_end contributes nothing. The left join keeps only flows strictly before the snapshot. A DROP has no byte count in the log; the running sum of signed ADD/REMOVE bytes up to the drop (the window function) is exactly what was active, and because a dropped table has no later events, subtracting it leaves zero.

Complexity. The spine join is O(days × events) in this form, which is fine for a sample and a few weeks; at scale, compute per-table daily deltas (bytes entering and leaving each state per day) and take running sums over days, which is O(events + days × tables) with no join between them.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: build the spine with GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => n) and DATEADD, DATEADD(day, retention_days, event_ts); the platform's own storage metrics views already report active, time-travel and fail-safe bytes per table (check current docs) — this exercise rebuilds them from a log. BigQuery: UNNEST(GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY(...)), TIMESTAMP_ADD(ts, INTERVAL n DAY). Spark SQL: explode(sequence(start, end, interval 1 day)), ts + make_interval(0, 0, 0, n). MySQL 8: a recursive CTE for the spine, DATE_ADD(ts, INTERVAL n DAY).

Edge cases built into the data. Every level: events weeks before the range whose bytes are still in fail-safe; tables with several retention values; a table may first appear during the range (zeros before). Hard: transient tables (retention 0 or 1, no fail-safe); a permanent table with retention 0 (straight to fail-safe); a removal at an exact midnight that reaches fail-safe exactly at a snapshot, another that is purged exactly at a snapshot, and an ADD exactly at a snapshot instant. Very Hard: one or two tables dropped during the range, with bytes NULL.

Common mistakes. Snapshot at the start of the day; <= at the end of a period; dropping fail-safe entirely or giving it to transient tables; only reporting days with events (no spine) or only tables with events; ignoring events before the range; treating NULL bytes on DROP as 0 (the SUM silently ignores it); computing active bytes with SUM(bytes) across all event types.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Under this model each chunk carries the retention in force when it was removed; a real platform documents how a change applies to data already in time travel (check current docs), so the log would need retention-change events and the rule for existing chunks. (2) Byte-days = sum of daily snapshots (or exact integration between events: bytes × seconds / 86 400); a daily sample misses data that lived less than a day; a bill is usually based on an average over the month. (3) Keep a daily state table per table and update it from yesterday's state plus today's events, plus the chunks whose periods end today (a calendar of tt_end/fs_end dates). (4) The 40 TB moved from active to time travel at the deletion, stays billed through retention and fail-safe, and leaves the bill only retention + 7 days later; give the dates and the expected curve.

Rubric anchors. 2: right totals for days with events, but no spine, or the boundaries are off by a day, or fail-safe is missing. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains the byte-day integration, an incremental daily state and the delayed bill drop with dates.

Strong signals. Draws the timeline for one removed chunk before writing SQL; asks whether period ends are inclusive; notices that a NULL in SUM disappears silently. Red flags. Claiming storage is freed at delete time; hard-coding table names or dates in CASE expressions.

import heapq
from collections import deque


def plan_warehouses(tasks, horizon):
    by_id = {t[0]: t for t in tasks}
    children = {}
    for t in tasks:
        for p in t[5]:
            children.setdefault(p, []).append(t[0])
    runs = []                                         # (start, task_id, size, end)
    for root, size, first, every, dur, after in tasks:
        if after:
            continue
        # The graph of this root in topological order (Kahn, within the graph).
        members, q = {root}, deque([root])
        while q:
            for c in children.get(q.popleft(), ()):
                if c not in members:
                    members.add(c)
                    q.append(c)
        indeg = {m: len(by_id[m][5]) for m in members}
        order, q = [], deque([root])
        while q:
            m = q.popleft()
            order.append(m)
            for c in children.get(m, ()):
                indeg[c] -= 1
                if indeg[c] == 0:
                    q.append(c)
        finish = None                                 # end of the last graph run that ran
        s = first
        while s < horizon:
            if finish is None or finish <= s:         # skip while the previous run is still going
                ends = {}
                for m in order:
                    t = by_id[m]
                    st = s if m == root else max(ends[p] for p in t[5])
                    ends[m] = st + t[4]
                    runs.append((st, m, t[1], ends[m]))
                finish = max(ends.values())
            s += every
    runs.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1]))
    busy, free, count, out = {}, {}, {}, []
    for st, tid, size, end in runs:
        b = busy.setdefault(size, [])
        f = free.setdefault(size, [])
        while b and b[0][0] <= st:                    # warehouses finished by now
            heapq.heappush(f, heapq.heappop(b)[1])
        if f:
            no = heapq.heappop(f)                     # lowest-numbered free warehouse
        else:
            no = count[size] = count.get(size, 0) + 1
        heapq.heappush(b, (end, no))
        out.append((tid, st, no))
    return count, out

Explanation. Two phases. Expansion: each root's schedule is walked minute by minute of its period (not minute by minute of the horizon); the skip rule needs only the end of the last graph run that ran, compared with <= because a run ending exactly at the next scheduled minute does not block it. For a standalone task the graph is just the root; for a graph, children are computed in a topological order of that graph so every predecessor's end is known, and the graph run's end is the maximum end of its members. Assignment: runs in (start, task_id) order; per size, a heap of busy (end, number) pairs releases every warehouse with end ≤ start into a heap of free numbers, and the smallest free number is taken, or a new one opened. This is classic interval partitioning: a new number is opened only when every open warehouse is busy at that start, so the count equals the peak number of simultaneous runs.

Complexity. O(R log R) time for R runs (the sort and the heap operations), O(R) memory for the output. The timing test (6 000 tasks over three days, about 85 000–140 000 runs, about 4 500 warehouses of one size busy at the peak) ran in 0.5–1.0 s in CPython; the same algorithm scanning warehouses 1, 2, 3, … for the first free one took 10–16 s.

Dialect notes. Java: PriorityQueue<int[]> for busy (end, no) and PriorityQueue<Integer> (or a TreeSet) for free numbers. C++: priority_queue with greater<>, or std::set<int> for free numbers. In SQL the count alone is a sweep (SUM(+1/−1) OVER (ORDER BY t) and its maximum); the lowest-free assignment is sequential and does not express well. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A warehouse freed at t reused at t; equal start times decided by task_id; the lowest free number when two are free (not the most recently freed); a run scheduled exactly at the horizon (not run); (Hard) sizes as separate pools; a run longer than its period (later runs skipped until it finishes); a run ending exactly at the next scheduled minute (not skipped); a run that starts before the horizon and ends after it; (Very Hard) a child with two predecessors of different lengths; an unfinished graph run that skips the next graph run while another task carries on; a graph run ending exactly at the next scheduled minute.

Common mistakes. <= horizon; skipping when the previous run ends exactly at the scheduled minute; shifting the schedule after a skip; treating [start, end] as closed; reusing the most recently freed warehouse (a stack) instead of the lowest number; one pool for all sizes; computing child starts in input order before their predecessors; applying the skip rule to the root alone instead of the whole graph run; a loop over every minute of the horizon for every task; scanning warehouses linearly.

Follow-up guidance. (1) At the moment the k-th warehouse opens, k − 1 warehouses are busy with runs that started at or before this start and end after it, so k runs overlap at that instant; hence k ≤ peak, and any assignment needs at least the peak. (2) With a resume cost and a minimum billed minute, short gaps are cheaper to bridge than to suspend; the objective becomes billed minutes, not warehouse count, and packing several small runs on one multi-cluster or larger warehouse may be cheaper (measure queueing). (3) Offsets: a local search or a min-max load heuristic over period slots; finding offsets that minimise the peak is hard in general, so state a heuristic and measure it against the lower bound ceil(Σ duration/every) per size. (4) Consolidate tasks with low concurrency and small working sets onto a shared warehouse; check queue time, run time and credits for a week before and after.

Rubric anchors. 2: right counts on samples but a closed interval, a wrong skip boundary, or a linear scan. 3: all tests pass with the two heaps per size. 4: also proves the greedy optimal and reasons about resume cost and offsets.

Strong signals. Separates schedule expansion from assignment; asks what happens to an overlapping run before coding; tests the lowest-number rule with a small hand case. Red flags. Simulating every minute of a three-day horizon for every task; claiming the count is the number of tasks.

def _glob(p):

        elif c == '?':

def simulate_warehouse(queries, policy):
    if not queries:
        return (0, 0, 0, 0, 0.0)
    slots = policy["slots"]
    lo, hi = policy["min_clusters"], policy["max_clusters"]
    startup, idle_s = policy["startup_s"], policy["idle_s"]

    t0 = queries[0][1]
    running = {}            # ready cluster id -> queries running on it
    idle_since = {}         # ready cluster id -> second it became idle (only while running == 0)
    started = {}            # cluster id -> second it started (billing)
    billed = 0
    for c in range(1, lo + 1):
        running[c] = 0
        idle_since[c] = t0
        started[c] = t0
    next_id = lo + 1
    starting = None         # (ready_at, id): at most one cluster starts at a time
    peak = lo

    finishes = []           # heap of (finish second, cluster id)
    queue = deque()
    i, n = 0, len(queries)
    max_wait = total_wait = 0
    t = t0
    while i < n or queue or finishes:
        # the next second at which anything can change
        cand = []
        if i < n:
            cand.append(queries[i][1])
        if finishes:
            cand.append(finishes[0][0])
        if starting:
            cand.append(starting[0])
        if len(running) + (1 if starting else 0) > lo:
            for c, s in idle_since.items():
                cand.append(max(s + idle_s, t))
        t = min(cand)

        # 1. finishes free their slots
        while finishes and finishes[0][0] == t:
            _, c = heapq.heappop(finishes)
            running[c] -= 1
            if running[c] == 0:
                idle_since[c] = t
        # 2. a starting cluster becomes ready
        if starting and starting[0] == t:
            c = starting[1]
            running[c] = 0
            idle_since[c] = t
            starting = None
        # 3. arrivals join the queue
        while i < n and queries[i][1] == t:
            queue.append(queries[i])
            i += 1
        # 4. dispatch to the lowest-numbered ready cluster with a free slot

            for c in sorted(running):

                    running[c] += 1

def best_join_order(tables, predicates, allow_cross=True):
    names = sorted(tables)
    n = len(names)
    if n == 0:
        return (0, [])
    pos = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(names)}
    pair = [[1] * n for _ in range(n)]       # product of the d's between two tables
    adj = [0] * n
    for a, b, d in predicates:
        i, j = pos[a], pos[b]
        pair[i][j] *= d
        pair[j][i] *= d
        adj[i] |= 1 << j
        adj[j] |= 1 << i
    full = (1 << n) - 1
    num = [1] * (full + 1)
    den = [1] * (full + 1)
    rows = [0] * (full + 1)
    for m in range(1, full + 1):
        low = m & -m
        j = low.bit_length() - 1
        rest = m ^ low
        num[m] = num[rest] * tables[names[j]]
        dd = den[rest]
        r = rest & adj[j]
        while r:
            lb = r & -r
            dd *= pair[j][lb.bit_length() - 1]
            r ^= lb
        den[m] = dd
        rows[m] = num[m] // dd                 # exact: multiply first, divide once
    single = [tables[t] for t in names]
    NONE = None
    best = [NONE] * (full + 1)                 # cheapest way to add the remaining tables to prefix set m
    best[full] = 0
    for m in range(full - 1, 0, -1):
        b = NONE
        rm = rows[m]
        free = full ^ m
        while free:
            lb = free & -free
            free ^= lb
            x = lb.bit_length() - 1
            if not allow_cross and not (adj[x] & m):
                continue
            nxt = best[m | lb]
            if nxt is NONE:
                continue
            c = rm + single[x] + rows[m | lb] + nxt
            if b is NONE or c < b:
                b = c
        best[m] = b
    first, cost = None, None
    for x in range(n):
        c = best[1 << x]
        if c is not None and (cost is None or c < cost):
            first, cost = x, c
    if first is None:
        return None
    order, m = [first], 1 << first
    while m != full:
        rm = rows[m]
        for x in range(n):                     # smallest name that stays optimal
            lb = 1 << x
            if m & lb or (not allow_cross and not (adj[x] & m)) or best[m | lb] is None:
                continue
            if rm + single[x] + rows[m | lb] + best[m | lb] == best[m]:
                order.append(x)
                m |= lb
                break
    return (cost, [names[i] for i in order])

Explanation. The cost of adding table x to a prefix set P is rows(P) + rows({x}) + rows(P ∪ {x}), and rows depends only on the set. So the cheapest way to finish a plan depends only on P: best[P] = min over x ∉ P of rows(P) + rows({x}) + rows(P ∪ {x}) + best[P ∪ {x}], with best[all] = 0. Supersets have larger bitmasks, so filling masks from the full set downwards always has best[P ∪ {x}] ready. The answer is the best single-table start. Rebuilding the order from the front, taking the smallest name that keeps the total optimal at each step, gives the lexicographically smallest optimal order, because names are indexed in sorted order. The row estimate of every subset is computed once, from the subset without its lowest table: the numerator gains that table's rows, and the denominator gains the d of its predicates into the rest. Multiplying first and dividing once keeps the floor exact, and Python integers do not overflow. With cross products forbidden, a transition needs a predicate between x and P; if no start reaches the full set, the answer is None.

Complexity. O(2ⁿ · n) transitions plus O(2ⁿ · deg) to build the estimates, and O(2ⁿ) memory. For 16 tables that is about a million transitions, and the reference takes about 0.4 s in CPython (0.06 s for 14 tables). Trying every order is 16! ≈ 2·10¹³. A DP that recomputes rows(S) from scratch on each transition is O(2ⁿ · n · (n + E)) and runs out of time at 16 tables.

import re

_IDENT = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*")
_SEGMENTS = {}


def _segment(key):
    if key not in _SEGMENTS:                       # keys repeat across records: decide once per key
        if _IDENT.fullmatch(key):                  # plain identifiers only; case is kept
            _SEGMENTS[key] = None
        else:
            _SEGMENTS[key] = '["' + key.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace('"', '\\"') + '"]'
    return _SEGMENTS[key]


def _walk(value, path, depth, max_depth, out):
    expand = max_depth is None or depth < max_depth          # a container at max_depth stays whole
    if isinstance(value, dict) and value and expand:
        for key, child in value.items():
            seg = _segment(key)
            if seg is not None:
                child_path = path + seg
            elif not path:
                child_path = key
            else:
                child_path = path + "." + key
            _walk(child, child_path, depth + 1, max_depth, out)
    elif isinstance(value, list) and value and expand:
        for i, child in enumerate(value):
            _walk(child, path + "[" + str(i) + "]", depth + 1, max_depth, out)
    else:
        out[path] = value                          # scalars, nulls, empty containers, depth-limited values


def flatten_records(records, max_depth=None):
    rows = []
    for record in records:
        out = {}
        for key, child in record.items():          # the record itself is never a leaf
            seg = _segment(key)
            _walk(child, key if seg is None else seg, 1, max_depth, out)
        rows.append(out)
    return rows

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Nulls are dropped. elif value is not None: skips JSON nulls, so a null field looks exactly like a missing one. Symptom: the data-quality rule "no orders have a null coupon" passes on data full of null coupons. Fix: keep None as a leaf.
  2. Empty objects and arrays vanish. An empty dict or list is expanded into zero children, so its path disappears. Symptom: customers with tags: [] drop out of the count by number of tags. Fix: treat an empty container as a leaf ({} or []). If the fix is applied inside _walk as written, an empty record becomes {"": {}}; the specification says the record itself is never a leaf, so the record must be handled by its own loop, as in the reference. The empty-record check catches exactly this.
  3. Keys are lower-cased. key = key.lower() with the comment "column names are case-insensitive". JSON keys are case-sensitive, so id and ID collide and the last one wins, and userId is reported as userid. Fix: keep the key as is. Case-folding is a decision for the column-discovery step, made with a collision rule, never silently here.
  4. Quoting only catches dots. _segment quotes a key only if it contains a dot, so ip address, x-ray and 2fa are written as if they were plain names, and a " inside a key is not escaped. Symptom: geo.ip address and ["x-ray"].on reported as x-ray.on, which the discovery job reads as nested fields. Fix: quote every key that is not an ASCII identifier, and escape \ and ".
  5. The depth limit is off by one. depth <= max_depth expands a container at exactly max_depth. Symptom: one extra level of columns with a depth limit set. Fix: depth < max_depth.

Each bug has its own check: a null, empty containers, id with ID, keys with a space, hyphen, leading digit or quote, and two depth-limit checks. A key with a dot passes on the original code, so a candidate who tests only that case will believe quoting works.

Explanation. Flattening is a walk over a tree, where each node's path is its parent's path plus one segment. The specification fixes what a leaf is (scalars, nulls, empty containers, and containers at the depth limit) and how a key becomes a segment. Everything else follows from applying those two rules consistently.

Complexity. O(total size of the documents) time and O(size of the output) memory. Path strings are built once per node. The timing test (15 000 documents, several hundred thousand leaves) runs in about half a second in CPython. Caching each key's segment avoids repeating the identifier check for keys that occur in every record.

Dialect notes. In a cloud warehouse the same flattening is usually done in SQL with a lateral flatten over the semi-structured column in recursive mode, which returns a path, key, index and value per element, and the platform's own path syntax uses : and dots or brackets with quoted keys. Its rules for nulls (a JSON null versus SQL NULL), empty arrays (an outer flatten keeps the parent row) and case are documented per product; check current docs. In Spark, explode and explode_outer differ in the same way for empty arrays. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Nested objects and arrays; nulls next to missing fields; empty objects and arrays; id with ID; a dotted key next to a nested key with the same letters; keys with a space, a hyphen and a leading digit; a quote inside a key; arrays of arrays; an empty record; a container at exactly max_depth; max_depth=1.

Common mistakes. Fixing nulls by keeping only None but still dropping False, 0 or "" with an if value:; fixing empty containers in a way that turns an empty record into {"": {}}; replacing the dot check with str.isidentifier(), which accepts non-ASCII letters; escaping quotes but not backslashes; changing the depth rule for arrays but not objects; rewriting the function from scratch instead of making minimal fixes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Infer a type per path from all values seen (the narrowest type that fits every value, with a variant or string fallback), keep the raw document, and route values that do not fit to a rejects column rather than dropping them. (2) Flatten an array into rows when consumers aggregate over its elements (line items); carry the parent's key and the array index onto each row so that it can be joined back and deduplicated. (3) Track the set of paths per source per day; a path that disappears while a similar one appears (same values, different case or separator) is a probable rename. Announce it, map both names during a transition window, and add a data contract. (4) Push the flatten into SQL over the semi-structured column for scale and pruning, and keep in code only the rules SQL cannot express well (quoting policy, collision rules, type inference), or express them as views.

Rubric anchors. 2: fixes two or three bugs; quoting or depth checks still fail. 3: all five fixed, all checks pass, each explained with its symptom. 4: also notices that fixing empty containers must not make an empty record a leaf, rejects case-folding with a reason, and adds a regression test per bug.

Strong signals. Writes the expected paths for a small document before touching the code; asks whether id and ID can both occur. Red flags. "Lower-case everything to be safe"; serialising nested values to strings so the tests pass.

SNO-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Discovery. Bucket event notifications feed a queue for low latency. A scheduled listing of each partner's prefix (for example hourly, by the bucket's own last-modified time) is reconciled against the manifest to catch lost or delayed notifications. Both write to the same manifest, so a file found twice is recorded once.
  • Manifest (your own load history). A table keyed by (path, checksum) with partner, size, first seen, load batch, status (discovered, loading, loaded, rejected, superseded), rows loaded and rows rejected. It never expires. It answers partner support and finance long after the platform's {{history_days}}-day history is gone.
  • Loading. Files are batched per partner and table into loads sized for the warehouse (for example tens to hundreds of megabytes of compressed data per file, and many files per load statement) rather than one load per tiny file. Small files are merged upstream where partners allow it, or loaded through a continuous ingestion service whose cost model suits small files. Each load is a transaction on a landing table that records the file name and row number per row. A failed load is retried; the platform's load history skips files already committed, and the manifest marks the rest.
  • Row-level idempotency. Landing is append-only with lineage. The modelled table is maintained by a MERGE on the partner's business key, keeping the row with the latest extract time, with the file name and row number as the deterministic tie-break. A re-sent file therefore changes nothing, a corrected file replaces exactly the rows it corrects, and a full re-send under new names is absorbed by the business key.
  • Older than the history. The pipeline never relies on the platform's history alone: before a forced or uncertain load, the manifest decides whether the (path, checksum) was already loaded. A file older than the history with an unknown status is loaded into landing and deduplicated by the merge.
  • Schema drift and bad rows. Per-partner schemas are versioned. New columns land in a semi-structured overflow column (or a rescue column) until mapped. Rows that fail parsing go to a rejects table with the file and line. One partner's drift never blocks another partner's loads.
  • Metrics and alerts. Files discovered versus loaded per partner and hour; discovery lag (listing finds a file notifications never reported); rows rejected; duplicates suppressed by the merge; files stuck in loading; daily row counts per partner against a baseline; credits per loaded gigabyte.

Competing designs to accept. Continuous ingestion driven by notifications plus a periodic listing sweep; scheduled bulk loads by prefix and date; an external orchestrator writing the manifest; a staging area outside the warehouse that compacts small files first. Any of them is fine if file-level and row-level idempotency are separate and the manifest outlives the platform's history.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Relying on the platform's load history as the only deduplication (it expires and is per table); forcing reloads; tiny files loaded one by one; notifications as the only discovery; merges without a deterministic tie rule; one partner's malformed file blocking a shared load; the manifest written outside the load's transaction, so a crash leaves it wrong.

Incident guidance.

  • A file from {{history_days}} days and one hour ago is re-uploaded unchanged: the platform can no longer tell, and may skip it or load it again depending on settings. The manifest knows the (path, checksum) was loaded, so the pipeline records the re-upload and skips it. If it is loaded by mistake, the merge on business key keeps the table correct. Partner support is told the file was already received on its original date.
  • A re-send and revenue up 9%: the re-sent rows reached the table additively, so the merge key or tie rule is wrong, or a downstream model reads landing rather than the merged table. Stop publication, compare the table's business keys against landing by file, fix the key (or the model that bypassed it), rebuild the affected days from landing, and add a monitor on duplicates per business key and on day-over-day totals per partner.
  • Notifications stop for six hours: there are no errors, so the alert must be on the listing sweep finding files the notifications did not report, and on row counts per partner against baseline. The sweep loads the missing files through the same path, and the manifest shows when each file was discovered and by which route.

Follow-up guidance. (1) A corrected file under the same name has a new checksum, so it is a new manifest entry and loads; the merge replaces the corrected rows. A full re-send under new names loads into landing and the merge absorbs it. Prove it with business-key counts and totals per day before and after. (2) List the affected prefixes for the window, diff against the manifest, and load the difference. Completeness comes from the listing, not from the notifications. (3) The partner's loads go to rejects or the overflow column while its schema is updated. Other partners are unaffected because loads and schemas are per partner. (4) From the manifest and landing lineage, which have no expiry. (5) Batch more files per load, ask partners to send fewer, larger files, compact before loading, and size the warehouse for the load and let it suspend between loads.

Rubric anchors. 2: relies on the platform's load history or file names alone; appends without a merge; no plan for files older than the history. 3: a durable manifest, landing with lineage, a merge on business key, listing behind notifications. 4: also a deterministic tie rule, a stated policy for uncertain files, per-partner isolation of drift, cost-aware batching, and monitors that detect silent failures.

Strong signals. Separates "was this file loaded" from "is this row present" in the first minutes; asks what identifies a partner's row. Red flags. "Use force and dedupe later" with no deduplication key; "notifications are reliable".

SNO-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Inventory and lineage. Catalogue every table, pipeline, query and consumer from the legacy system's query logs and job scheduler, with owners and usage. Unused tables are retired, not migrated. Group the rest into domains (for example sales reporting, finance extracts, a product team's application) with their full lineage.
  • Order. Start with a low-risk domain that exercises the hard parts (types, incremental loads, a few dashboards), then the high-value domains, and the most coupled ones last. Each domain moves through the same gates: copied, catching up, translated, reconciled, cut over, legacy read-only, legacy retired.
  • Copy and catch-up. An initial bulk export to object storage and load into the cloud platform, then incremental catch-up. For append-only tables, by load date. For tables updated in place, by change capture or a modified-timestamp column where trustworthy, or by periodic snapshot comparison of partitions. Extraction runs off-peak, rate-limited, on the legacy system.
  • Translation. An automated translator for most SQL, plus tests per query: run both sides on the same snapshot and compare results. A list of known dialect traps (NULL versus empty string, integer division, decimal scale and rounding, timestamp types and time zones, case sensitivity of identifiers and comparisons, string collation) gets its own tests.
  • Dual running and reconciliation. While legacy is the source of truth, the cloud pipelines run on the same inputs. Reconciliation runs per table and per business date at three grains: row counts; aggregates of key measures by partition and key dimensions; and, where those disagree, a row-level hash over a canonical form (normalised decimals, timestamps in UTC, an explicit NULL token). Every difference is classified (translation, data movement, a known rule, or a legacy defect) and tracked to closure. Tolerances are per measure, documented and signed off by its owner.
  • Cutover and rollback. Consumers read through a switchable layer (a connection profile, a DNS name, or views in a semantic layer), so a cutover is a configuration change. Each consumer is cut over after its own acceptance check, with its owner, and can be switched back within minutes while legacy stays read-only and current.
  • Switch-off. When every consumer is cut over and stable for an agreed period, legacy stops loading, a final reconciliation runs, the data needed for audit is archived to object storage in an open format with its schema, and the system is decommissioned.
  • Reporting. Weekly numbers: tables and consumers by gate, reconciliation pass rate and open differences by class and age, query translation coverage, parallel-running cost to date, and the forecast date per domain against {{deadline}}.

Competing designs to accept. A big-bang cutover for a small estate with a strong rollback plan; replicating the legacy data continuously with a CDC tool; re-platforming pipelines first and backfilling history later; rebuilding the model rather than lifting and shifting, if the candidate prices the extra risk. Each has trade-offs in risk, cost and calendar time.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Extraction load on legacy; in-place updates missed by incremental copies; translations that run without errors but return different answers; reconciliation that compares row counts only; consumers owned by other teams that never test; open-ended parallel running that doubles the cost; switching off before archiving.

Incident guidance.

  • A 0.02% revenue difference where legacy was wrong: classify it as a legacy defect, get finance to agree which number is right, document it, and decide whether to restate past reports. Add a reconciliation rule that expects the difference, so it is not re-raised. The lesson is that reconciliation finds differences, and people decide which side is right.
  • A reconciliation query slows the morning reports: stop it, move reconciliation to an off-peak window with a resource limit or workload class on legacy, and run heavy comparisons from exported snapshots instead of live queries.
  • 4% of consumers not cut over ten days before the deadline: escalate with the list, owners and the consequences. Offer cutover with rollback in the remaining days, temporarily repoint untested consumers with their owners' sign-off, or agree a short, priced extension of legacy for named consumers. Never switch off silently.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Narrow by grain: which dates, which keys. Then compare the translated SQL against the original for rounding, filters and time zones, compare the copied source rows, and check whether legacy itself has a known defect. (2) Use change capture or an updated-at column. If neither is reliable, reconcile partitions by hash and recopy those that differ, and freeze in-place updates during the final cutover window. (3) Cut scope (retire more tables, move low-use consumers as-is), add people to translation and testing, and keep the reconciliation and rollback gates; never skip reconciliation to save time. (4) All consumers cut over and stable, no open unexplained differences, archives verified by restoring a sample, and sign-off from owners and audit. (5) The weekly numbers above, with trends.

Rubric anchors. 2: copy everything and switch over a weekend; reconciliation by row counts; no rollback. 3: domain-by-domain plan with lineage, catch-up, multi-grain reconciliation and reversible cutovers. 4: also classified differences with owners, dialect traps tested on purpose, cost and capacity of parallel running managed, and honest, measurable reporting.

Strong signals. Asks how consumers connect before planning cutover; insists that legacy can be wrong too. Red flags. "The translator handles it"; turning legacy off on the deadline regardless of what is left.

SNO-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Default: shared tables with a tenant key, plus dedicated objects for outliers (a hybrid).
    • tenants (tenant_id, name, region, tier shared|dedicated, created_at, offboarding_requested_at).
    • tickets (tenant_id, ticket_id, created_at, channel, priority, status, requester_key, assignee_agent_id, …), ticket_events (tenant_id, ticket_id, event_id, event_type, actor, occurred_at), agents (tenant_id, agent_id, team, valid_from, valid_to), surveys (tenant_id, ticket_id, score, responded_at). Every key is composite with tenant_id first, so no join can cross tenants by accident.
    • Clustering: shared fact tables clustered by (tenant_id, event date); tiny tenants share micro-partitions, the largest tenant's rows fill their own, so its queries prune well. The largest tenant ({{largest_share}} of rows) is the strongest candidate to move to dedicated objects and its own warehouse.
  • Enforcement on every read path.
    • One row access policy attached to every shared table, mapping the session's context to allowed tenant ids: for the dashboard service, a tenant id set by the service per request (session variable or query tag) and checked against a mapping table of the service's roles; for direct tenant access, a role per tenant (or a share to the tenant's own account with a secure view filtered by the consumer account); for internal analysts, no row access except through aggregated, thresholded views.
    • Dashboards query only secure views over the policy-protected tables, so view definitions and filters cannot be inspected or bypassed.
    • The result cache and the service's own cache key must include the tenant context; exports go through the same views.
  • Custom fields ({{custom_fields}}). custom_field_defs (tenant_id, field_id, name, type, status, created_at, retired_at) and either a typed key-value table ticket_custom_values (tenant_id, ticket_id, field_id, value_text, value_number, value_date) or a semi-structured column keyed by field_id (never by display name, so renames are free). For dashboard performance, a per-tenant pivot view or materialisation of the few fields a tenant actually filters on.
  • Deletion. Shared tables: delete by tenant_id (a large DML job), then time travel and any recovery retention must lapse before the data is gone everywhere; state the window. Dedicated schema or database: drop it, with the same retention caveat. Evidence: a deletion job record with row counts per table and the date recovery copies expire.
  • Residency ({{regions}}). A separate account (or deployment) per region; tenants live in exactly one; cross-region analytics only on aggregates.
  • Cost attribution. Compute: per-query credits allocated from warehouse metering by execution time within each warehouse-hour, attributed to the tenant id carried in the query tag; storage: bytes per tenant from table sizes (dedicated) or row-share estimates (shared). Heavy direct-query tenants get their own warehouse, billed to them directly.

Competing designs to accept. Pure schema-per-tenant at low tenant counts (hundreds), if they automate migrations with per-tenant version tracking and accept object-count limits and slower onboarding. Database-per-tenant with data sharing to each tenant's own account for the large ones. Pure shared tables with secure views only (no row access policy) if the views are the only grant and the tenant context cannot be forged. Application-side filtering is not acceptable as the only control.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Tenant context passed by a service that can be wrong or forged; caches keyed without tenant; object explosion at {{tenants}} schemas (migrations, grants, metadata); tiny tenants' rows scattered across partitions without tenant clustering; the largest tenant starving others on a shared warehouse; deletion that ignores recovery copies; custom fields keyed by display name.

Incident guidance.

  • Cached result served across tenants: treat as a data exposure. Disable the cache path, identify affected queries from the query log (same query text, different tenant context, cache hit), notify affected tenants. Fix: include tenant context in every cache key and enforce the filter in the database (row access policy) so a cache hit can only return data the policy allowed for that session. Guardrail: an automated test that runs the same dashboard as two tenants and diffs results; at {{tenants}} tenants, sample continuously.
  • Schemas left a column behind after a failed release: per-schema migration state was not tracked. Record a schema version per tenant, make migrations idempotent and resumable, block a deploy until all schemas report the target version, and roll forward the stragglers. This is a cost of schema-per-tenant worth naming.
  • Largest tenant starving small tenants: move its direct queries to its own warehouse (or a multi-cluster warehouse with limits), add resource monitors and statement timeouts, and consider moving the tenant to dedicated objects; measure dashboard latency per tenant tier.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Policy: if the role is the dashboard service role, allow rows where tenant_id = the per-request context and the mapping table confirms it; if a tenant role, allow its tenant; if an analyst role, deny raw rows. (2) Clustering by (tenant_id, date) prunes both; a tiny tenant reads a few partitions shared with others, the largest reads its own. (3) Shared: delete DML plus waiting out retention; dedicated: drop plus retention; evidence either way. (4) Shared: one ALTER; per-tenant: a migration fan-out with versions and retries. (5) Allocate warehouse-hour credits by tenant-tagged execution time; idle time as a shared overhead line.

Rubric anchors. 2: "add a tenant_id column and filter in the app"; no answer for direct access or caches. 3: a policy-enforced shared model or automated per-tenant schemas with clear trade-offs, custom fields designed, deletion and cost attribution addressed. 4: also a hybrid with a promotion rule, residency, cache and export paths, clustering for skew, recovery-copy-aware deletion and crisp incident handling.

Strong signals. Enumerates read paths before choosing; treats the service account as a threat. Red flags. Isolation by naming convention; one warehouse for everything with no limits; custom fields as new columns on the shared table per tenant request.

SNO-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Landing. raw_events (event_id, event_type, device_id, user_id, app_version, device_ts, received_ts, event_date (derived from received_ts or a corrected time), payload semi-structured, file_name, file_row, loaded_at, schema_fingerprint). Envelope fields are typed at load; the payload stays semi-structured; nothing is rejected at this layer. Clustered by event_date (and event_type if most queries filter on it). Kept for a stated replay period.
  • Typed layer. For the dozen hot event types, one table each with typed columns extracted by a versioned rule (extraction_version), e.g. workouts (event_id, user_id, device_id, started_at, duration_s, distance_m, calories, app_version, event_date). Values that fail typing go to a rejects table (event_id, path, raw_value, expected_type, app_version, rule_version) and are counted per load; the typed column is NULL with a flag, never silently NULL.
  • Flattened children. heart_rate_samples (event_id, idx, offset_s, bpm) at sample grain, and workout_laps (event_id, lap_no, …); keyed by event id and index so reloads are idempotent.
  • Null versus missing. Keep a presence flag (or keep JSON nulls in the payload, which the platform can distinguish from absence) for fields where the distinction matters; typed columns document which they mean.
  • Drift. Each load profiles paths and their types per event type and app version against a registry; new paths are listed (analysts can query them from the raw payload the same day), type changes raise alerts and route values to rejects; promotions of a path to a typed column are reviewed changes with a new extraction version and a backfill.
  • Contract. A versioned schema per event type, owned by the app team, with compatibility rules (add optional fields freely; never change a type or meaning under the same name; renames are add-new, deprecate-old); old app versions are mapped by app_version.

Competing designs to accept. One table per event type created automatically from the registry (if they handle the long tail and cross-type queries). A fully flattened wide table for a small, stable set of types. Schema-on-read only with views over the raw table, at small scale, if they show how they would detect drift and keep pruning on typed columns.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Path expressions on the payload for time filters (no pruning); exploding large arrays for every query; casts that NULL bad values; mixed types under one path reducing the benefit of columnar storage of the semi-structured column; dashboards reading raw paths; device clocks used as the partition date.

Incident guidance.

  • distance became a string; typed column NULLed it: contain by flagging the affected app version's rows on dashboards; fix by routing failed casts to rejects with counts and alerting on a reject rate above a threshold per version; parse the new format under a new path or rule version and backfill from raw. Guardrail: a per-version type check in the load.
  • Full scan on a string timestamp: teach the typed event_date column (clustered) and expose views that filter on it; reject or rewrite dashboards that filter on payload paths. At {{daily_events}} events a day, show the scanned-partition ratio before and after.
  • Renamed field split across versions: a mapping in the extraction rule coalesces old and new names by app version into one typed column; dashboards read the typed column only; the contract forbids renames without a deprecation period. With {{drift}}, the registry should surface renames as "new path + vanishing path in the same type".

Follow-up guidance. (1) {{daily_events}} × 2% × 1,800 samples a day: cluster by event_date and user or device, keep raw samples for a limited period and per-minute aggregates longer. (2) New rule version, rejects for the old parse, backfill from raw, typed column unchanged in meaning. (3) Raw payload path today; promotion to a typed column through a reviewed change. (4) A check that envelope user_id is non-null per app version, compared with the prior version's rate. (5) Wide table: few stable types; per type: hot types; envelope + payload + children: the long tail and drift.

Rubric anchors. 2: everything in one semi-structured column queried directly, or everything flattened with failed casts dropped. 3: typed envelope, raw payload kept, typed tables for hot types, children for arrays, drift detection with rejects. 4: also null-versus-missing, versioned extraction with backfill, pruning designed, contract that copes with old clients, and sized estimates.

Strong signals. Asks which queries dominate before deciding what to flatten; treats drift as measured data. Red flags. "Cast and move on"; partitioning by device clock; no raw retention for replay.

SNO-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Facts.
    • fct_sales_line (one row per sold line on a receipt): date_key, store_key, product_key, member_key (nullable → "anonymous" member), currency_code, receipt_id, line_no, quantity, gross_minor, discount_minor, net_minor (transaction currency), sold_at.
    • fct_return_line (one row per returned line): return date, store_key of the returning store, product_key, quantity, refund_minor, currency, original receipt and line when known (original_sale_line_id nullable), return_type with_receipt|without_receipt. Alternatively signed rows in one fact with a line_type; both are fine if the grain is stated.
    • fct_line_promotion (one row per line × promotion): the promotion's own discount on that line from the point-of-sale system, so discount cost by promotion sums exactly; or a bridge with allocation weights summing to 1 per line for sales attribution.
  • Dimensions. Date; store (type 2: region, format, franchise flag, with valid_from/valid_to, plus a type 1 "current region" column for "as is"); product (type 2 for category changes); member; promotion (type, mechanics, start/end); currency.
  • Currency. Amounts stored in transaction currency minor units; fx_rates (currency, rate_date, rate_to_group, version, published_at); group-currency values computed in a view at the transaction date's latest rate version, or materialised with the rate version recorded so a correction is a targeted recompute.
  • Late stores. On first sight of an unknown code, insert an inferred store row (code, currency, is_inferred = true, placeholder attributes) and load the sales against its surrogate key; when master data arrives (up to {{store_lag_days}} days later), update the inferred row in place (type 1 for the placeholder period) and open type 2 history from then on. Sales never move keys.
  • Net sales definition. Σ net sales lines in the month − Σ refunds of returns processed in the month (activity basis), in group currency at each transaction's own date rate; returns without receipt counted at the refunded amount; a return-rate view by sale-month cohort is separate.

Competing designs to accept. One signed fact for sales and returns with a line-type column. Converting at load if the rate version is stored and a correction triggers a targeted restatement. A single "unknown" member plus a remapping job, if they show the remap updates facts' keys reliably (weaker but acceptable with a reconciliation check).

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Grain unstated (receipt versus line); promotion bridges double-counting; currency converted at load without a version; unknown stores mapped to one default member and never remapped; "as is" versus "as was" confusion when stores change region; at {{daily_lines}} lines a day, facts clustered on a key nobody filters on.

Incident guidance.

  • Late store's sales stuck on the "unknown" member: the single default member lost the store code. Remap facts by store code for the affected days (or, better, switch to inferred members keyed by code), restate the region's like-for-like with a note, and add a check that unknown-member sales are zero after {{store_lag_days}} days plus a margin.
  • Promotion discount exceeding receipt discount by 18%: the bridge repeated the full line discount per promotion. Use per-promotion discount rows from the point-of-sale data (or allocation weights summing to 1), restate the promotion report, and add a reconciliation: Σ discount by promotion = Σ discount on receipts per day.
  • Late rate load: conversion at load used the stale rate. Recompute group-currency values for the affected date and currency from the corrected rate version, publish a restatement with the delta, and gate loads that need a rate on the rate being present for that date (or convert in a view).

Follow-up guidance. (1) As in the definition above, with the treatment of cross-month returns stated. (2) Per-promotion discount rows answer cost; lift needs a baseline and the line counted once (distinct line keys). (3) The inferred member shows the code and "pending registration"; attributes fill in when master data lands; no fact moves. (4) Recompute conversions for that date and currency, or nothing if conversion is a view; reports carry the rate version. (5) Cluster by date (and store for store-level reports); most queries filter by date range and store or region.

Rubric anchors. 2: one wide sales table with converted amounts and a promo_id column. 3: stated grains, conformed dimensions with SCD choices, promotions without double-counting, inferred members, currency kept in transaction currency. 4: also "as was" and "as is" queries, reproducible conversion with versions, return linkage including no-receipt returns, and restatement discipline.

Strong signals. States both grains first; reaches for inferred members unprompted. Red flags. Holding sales until the store exists; summing amounts across currencies; deleting and reloading closed months silently.

SNO-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Query fact. fct_query (query_id, start_time, end_time, warehouse_id, user_id, role_id, team_id (from tag or mapping, with source), fingerprint_id, status, error_class, compilation_ms, queued_provisioning_ms, queued_overload_ms, blocked_ms, execution_ms, bytes_scanned, partitions_scanned, partitions_total, rows_produced, query_tag, loaded_at). One row per query id; loaded by MERGE over a window wider than {{history_latency}} plus the longest query, so a running record is updated, never duplicated.
  • Text. query_text (query_id, text) in a restricted schema; dim_fingerprint (fingerprint_id, normalised_text, first_seen, last_seen) readable by all. Fingerprint = hash of the text with literals, whitespace, comments and IN-list lengths normalised; collisions between different reports are rare but possible, and parameter-dependent plans share one fingerprint.
  • Warehouse dimension. Type 2 from a settings-change log or snapshots: size, min/max clusters, scaling policy, auto-suspend seconds, valid_from/valid_to; queries join on start_time within validity.
  • Metering and allocation. fct_warehouse_metering (warehouse_id, hour, credits) from the platform; fct_query_cost (query_id, warehouse_id, hour, allocated_credits): each warehouse-hour's credits split across the queries that executed in it by execution time overlapping the hour (weighted by cluster count if multi-cluster), plus an idle row per warehouse-hour for the remainder so Σ allocated = metered exactly.
  • Aggregates. agg_warehouse_hour (warehouse_id, hour, queries, queued_overload_ms, queued_provisioning_ms, execution_ms, credits), agg_fingerprint_day, agg_team_month. Full grain kept {{retention_days}} days; aggregates for years.

Competing designs to accept. Storing raw history rows append-only and deduplicating in a view by latest record per query id (if the view is what everyone reads). Allocation by bytes scanned or by elapsed time, if stated and reconciled. Snapshotting warehouse settings hourly instead of a change log.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Watermarks on end time with delayed history; duplicate rows for running queries; current-size joins; one queued number hiding cold starts; idle credit dropped so chargebacks do not sum to the bill; query text broadly readable; fingerprints that over- or under-merge.

Incident guidance.

  • Watermark skipped a day of queries: the watermark ignored the {{history_latency}} delay. Reload the window with a MERGE (idempotent), restate team spend for the week, and change the load to re-read a lookback window ≥ the delay; add a check that daily query counts per warehouse match the platform's own counts, across {{warehouses}} warehouses.
  • Cost per fingerprint recomputed at the new size: the warehouse dimension was type 1. Rebuild size history from the change log (or metering, which reflects the size then), recompute last quarter, and issue chargeback corrections as adjustments rather than editing invoices. Guardrail: costs come from metering allocated per hour, never from size × time at current settings.
  • More clusters for a provisioning queue: the metric mixed provisioning and overload queueing. Split them; provisioning queues point at auto-suspend and warm-up, overload queues at size or clusters; revert the change and monitor both measures.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Queued share = Σ queued_overload_ms ÷ Σ (queued_overload_ms + execution_ms) for queries started in the hour; persistent overload with many concurrent small queries argues for more clusters, few long queries spilling argue for a bigger size. (2) 60 minutes of credits: 10/20/30 minutes of execution get 1/6, 2/6, 3/6 of the active share, and the idle 20 minutes are a separate line (or spread proportionally, if stated). (3) Normalise literals, whitespace, comments and IN lists; risks: different reports that differ only in literals merge, dynamic SQL with varying column lists splits. (4) MERGE on query id over [watermark − delay − max duration, now); the watermark is the min of the source's completeness marker and now − delay. (5) {{daily_queries}} × {{retention_days}} rows at full grain, clustered by start date and warehouse; daily aggregates retained longer.

Rubric anchors. 2: an append-only copy of history with total elapsed time and current warehouse size. 3: query grain with MERGE, time components separate, type 2 warehouse settings, fingerprints, allocation that reconciles. 4: also both queueing kinds driving different actions, text access control, delay-aware watermarking, idle credit explicit and sized retention.

Strong signals. Asks how queueing is broken down; insists allocated credits sum to metering. Red flags. Cost = elapsed time × current size; dropping failed queries; everyone can read query text.

SNO-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{report_end}} is the instance's report end)

WITH rs AS (                      -- RESUME and SUSPEND before report_end, with the previous one's type
  SELECT warehouse_name, event_type, occurred_at,
         LAG(event_type) OVER (PARTITION BY warehouse_name ORDER BY occurred_at) AS prev_type
  FROM warehouse_events
  WHERE event_type IN ('RESUME', 'SUSPEND')
    AND occurred_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '{{report_end}}'
), eff AS (                       -- only events that change the state; a warehouse starts suspended
  SELECT warehouse_name, event_type, occurred_at
  FROM rs
  WHERE event_type <> COALESCE(prev_type, 'SUSPEND')
), runs AS (
  SELECT warehouse_name, event_type, occurred_at AS resumed_at,
         COALESCE(LEAD(occurred_at) OVER (PARTITION BY warehouse_name ORDER BY occurred_at),
                  TIMESTAMPTZ '{{report_end}}') AS ended_at
  FROM eff
), billed AS (
  SELECT warehouse_name, resumed_at, ended_at,
         LEAST(GREATEST(ended_at, resumed_at + INTERVAL '60 seconds'),
               TIMESTAMPTZ '{{report_end}}') AS billed_end
  FROM runs
  WHERE event_type = 'RESUME'
), sizes AS (                     -- the size in force from each change until the next
  SELECT warehouse_name, from_at, size,
         LEAD(from_at, 1, TIMESTAMPTZ 'infinity') OVER (PARTITION BY warehouse_name ORDER BY from_at) AS to_at
  FROM (
    SELECT warehouse_name, TIMESTAMPTZ '-infinity' AS from_at, initial_size AS size FROM warehouses
    UNION ALL
    SELECT warehouse_name, occurred_at, size
    FROM warehouse_events
    WHERE event_type = 'RESIZE' AND occurred_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '{{report_end}}'
  ) z
), segs AS (
  SELECT b.warehouse_name,                       -- running time, cut at each resize
         GREATEST(b.resumed_at, s.from_at) AS seg_start,
         LEAST(b.ended_at, s.to_at) AS seg_end, s.size
  FROM billed b
  JOIN sizes s ON s.warehouse_name = b.warehouse_name
              AND s.from_at < b.ended_at AND s.to_at > b.resumed_at
  UNION ALL
  SELECT b.warehouse_name, b.ended_at, b.billed_end, s.size   -- the minimum's padding, at the run's last size
  FROM billed b
  JOIN sizes s ON s.warehouse_name = b.warehouse_name
              AND s.from_at < b.ended_at AND s.to_at >= b.ended_at
  WHERE b.billed_end > b.ended_at
), hourly AS (
  SELECT g.warehouse_name, h.hour_start, ws.credits_per_hour,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM LEAST(g.seg_end, h.hour_start + INTERVAL '1 hour')
                          - GREATEST(g.seg_start, h.hour_start))::BIGINT AS secs
  FROM segs g
  JOIN warehouse_sizes ws ON ws.size = g.size
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(date_trunc('hour', g.seg_start),
                                     g.seg_end - INTERVAL '1 microsecond',
                                     INTERVAL '1 hour') AS h(hour_start)
  WHERE g.seg_end > g.seg_start
)
SELECT warehouse_name, hour_start,
       SUM(secs) AS billed_seconds,
       ROUND(SUM(secs * credits_per_hour) / 3600.0, 4) AS credits
FROM hourly
WHERE secs > 0
GROUP BY warehouse_name, hour_start
ORDER BY warehouse_name, hour_start;

Explanation. The log is a state machine, so it is first reduced to effective transitions: with a warehouse starting suspended, an event changes the state exactly when its type differs from the previous RESUME/SUSPEND (this drops a RESUME while running and a SUSPEND while suspended; at Medium and Hard there are none, so the step is harmless). LEAD then pairs each effective RESUME with its SUSPEND, or with report_end if the run is still open. Each run's billed end is the later of its end and resume + 60 s, capped at report_end, so the minimum is paid per resume and two minimums can overlap. Sizes become intervals (the initial size from −infinity, each RESIZE until the next); running time is intersected with them, and the padding gets the size in force when the run ended (the data never resizes during a padding, so intersecting the padding with size intervals gives the same answer). Finally each segment is cut at hour boundaries with generate_series; seconds × rate are summed as integers and divided and rounded once per row.

Complexity. Two window sorts over the events per warehouse, a join of runs to size intervals (each run meets only the intervals it overlaps), and one generated row per hour a segment touches. Incrementally in production: carry each warehouse's open run, current size and last resume time across loads, and recompute only hours touched since the last watermark minus the log's delay.

Dialect notes. Snowflake: TIMEADD/DATEADD('second', 60, ts), DATE_TRUNC('HOUR', ts), and no generate_series over timestamps — split hours with a numbers table (TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => n))) or a calendar table of hours joined on overlap; CONDITIONAL_CHANGE_EVENT or LAG can drop no-op events; TIMESTAMP_TZ literals as '…'::TIMESTAMP_TZ. BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_ADD, TIMESTAMP_TRUNC(ts, HOUR), GENERATE_TIMESTAMP_ARRAY(start, end, INTERVAL 1 HOUR) with UNNEST; no infinity timestamps, so use far-past/far-future literals. Spark SQL: sequence(date_trunc('HOUR', s), e, INTERVAL 1 HOUR) with explode, and unix_timestamp differences for seconds. MySQL 8: a recursive CTE or an hours table for the split; TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, a, b). In engines where GREATEST/LEAST return NULL for any NULL argument (Snowflake, BigQuery), the COALESCE to report_end matters. None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. A run shorter than 60 s (billed 60 s); a run of exactly 60 s (no padding); two runs whose minimums overlap (both billed); a short run near the end of an hour whose padding spills into the next hour; a run resuming exactly at hh:00:00 and suspending exactly at a later hh:00:00 (nothing in the final hour); runs spanning two or three hours. Hard adds RESIZE events inside long runs, a RESIZE inside a run shorter than the minimum (the padding bills at the new size), and a RESIZE while suspended (the next run starts at that size). Very Hard adds a RESUME while running (inside the first minute, so restarting the minimum changes the bill, and inside a long run), a SUSPEND while suspended, a run open at report_end with its SUSPEND after it, a run resumed seconds before report_end (its minimum is cut at report_end), and a whole run after report_end.

Common mistakes. No minimum; merging overlapping minimums into one interval; charging the whole run (or just the padding) to the resume hour; ignoring resizes during runs or while suspended; (Very Hard) treating a duplicate RESUME as a new start; using events after report_end; dropping open runs. Each has a diagnostic. Also common: pairing with LEAD over all events (a RESIZE becomes the run's end), rounding per segment, and off-by-one on the hour boundary (<= in generate_series end produces a zero-second row, filtered here by secs > 0).

Follow-up guidance. (1) Differences with metering: runs still open or late SUSPENDs at the cut-off; resize billing (in the real product a resize may bill differently — check current docs); multi-cluster warehouses; cloud-services credits; time zone of the hour buckets; the log's delivery delay and duplicates. (2) padding credits = credits on padding segments per warehouse ÷ total; recommend longer auto-suspend or consolidating probes onto a warehouse that is already running. (3) Runs per cluster: events carry a cluster number, and each cluster's start pays its own minimum; the warehouse's credits are the sum over clusters. (4) Carry state per warehouse (open run's resume time, current size, whether the minimum is already paid); recompute hours from the earliest late event's timestamp; finance reads only hours older than the log's delay.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but no minimum, or no split at hours, or runs paired by naive LEAD over all events. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains the metering differences, how to make it incremental, and the padding-waste query.

Strong signals. Builds runs and size intervals as separate steps; asks whether minimums overlap before writing code. Red flags. Summing EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM ended_at - resumed_at) per run start hour; rounding each run; filtering events by date only, so runs crossing midnight or report_end break.
